newsitem.title: MEXICO: Colombian Nobel laureate turns 70 in solitude.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Nobel laureate turns 70 in solitude.

text.p: Colombian Nobel literature laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez celebrated his 70th birthday on Thursday in the kind of quirky, self-imposed solitude enjoyed -- or suffered -- by characters who people his best-selling novels.

Attempts to reach the 1982 Nobel prize winner, whose novel "One Hundred Years of Solitude" has sold 20 million copies in 18 languages, ran into a wall of silence and misdirection as "Gabo" exiled himself not only from his homeland but from the world.
"He is not in Mexico ... nor will he be celebrating his birthday in Mexico," a woman answering the telephone at his home in the Mexico City suburb of Jardines de Pedregal told Reuters.
But a close friend of Marquez said, "He is not in Mexico City but he might be in Cuernavaca," referring to a weekend getaway city near the Mexican capital. "Or maybe in Cuba?"
Friends and family members said this week the world's most renowned Colombian was unlikely to mark his birthday in his violence-torn homeland, where he currently refuses to live.

In a statement to Colombia's RCN radio network on Feb. 19, explaining why he had left his homes in Bogota and Cartagena, if only temporarily, Garcia Marquez alluded to threats to his personal safety. "The situation in Colombia has become uncomfortable, insecure and uneasy," he said. "I left to find a place where I can do what I can do for Colombia, which is write."
The former reporter and encyclopaedia salesman spends most of his time in Mexico these days but has lived in Cuba and elsewhere for most of the past 40 years.

"Congratulations, brother!" Mexican novelist Carlos Fuentes said in a brief message to his literary friend published by the newspaper La Jornada. "It is enough just to open one of your marvellous books to be born again, 70 years ago, and to begin to live, 70 years later."
Garcia Marquez was born on March 6, 1927, in the small town of Aracataca, in Colombia's northern province of Magdalena.

Thursday also marked the 30th anniversary of the first publication of "One Hundred Years of Solitude" in Buenos Aires -- it sold out in two weeks -- and the 50th anniversary of the publication of his first short story, "The Third Resignation," in the Bogota newspaper El Espectador.
